entities.summary:
Noreay Reachea (b. 1418, d. 1468), a prominent monarch of the Khmer Kingdom, navigated a period of profound transition and vulnerability in Southeast Asia during the 15th century. His reigns (1438–1444 and 1446–1458) were defined by the strategic imperative to consolidate power and establish new administrative centers following the abandonment of Angkor, a move necessitated by persistent Siamese incursions and environmental shifts. As the son of King Ponhea Yat, who first relocated the capital to Phnom Penh, Noreay Reachea inherited the challenge of redefining Khmer sovereignty in a post-Angkorian landscape, making his era critical for the subsequent trajectory of Cambodian statehood.

During his first reign, Noreay Reachea continued the efforts to stabilize the kingdom, primarily from the new capital at Phnom Penh. His rule was punctuated by ongoing military engagements with the powerful Ayutthaya Kingdom, which exerted significant pressure on Khmer territories. A period of internal dynastic conflict saw him temporarily deposed by his brother, Reamea Thipadei, only to regain the throne in 1446. Upon his return, he further experimented with capital locations, briefly moving the administrative center to Srei Santhor, reflecting the fluid and often precarious geopolitical situation that defined 15th-century Cambodia. These shifts were not merely architectural but represented a strategic recalibration of power away from the vulnerable, grand scale of Angkor.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Noreay Reachea's reign marked a crucial transitional period for the Khmer kingdom, as he navigated persistent Siamese invasions and strategically relocated administrative centers, thereby consolidating a post-Angkorian identity and ensuring the continuity of the Cambodian monarchy. His actions were instrumental in preserving Khmer statehood and culture in the face of regional hegemons.
